sentences.text: From exports to an analysis ready data set: exporting, checking, cleaning, and merging iMotions data
This workshop turns the files that iMotions Lab 11 point 1 writes into one table you can test.

You will plan which export holds which measure, get every export out, open each file without breaking it, check it, clean it, merge it, document every decision, and run three hypothesis tests on the result.
Every section explains why before how.

An analysis ready data set has three properties: one row per unit of analysis (in the worked example, one participant watching one stimulus), one column per variable, and every value traceable to a raw export and a logged decision.
iMotions does not write such a table.
It writes families of files, and each answers one question at one level:
Sensor Data: every sample of every selected sensor on one timeline, one file per respondent, below lines of study information.
A O I metrics: gaze and fixation measures for each area of interest (A O I), a region drawn on a stimulus, per respondent or averaged over everyone.
F E A metrics: how much of each stimulus a facial expression scored by Affectiva aff decks stayed above a threshold, per respondent.
G S R Peak Metrics: peaks of skin conductance (G S R) per respondent and stimulus, with the length of usable signal.
Survey: every answer of every respondent in one matrix, and a file of summary statistics.
Data quality: the data quality file, with each device's sampling rate and percent of data obtained per respondent and stimulus.
Annotations: the start, end, and duration of each marked time window, an annotation.
The A O I, F E A, and G S R files come from the R Processing tab of the analysis Export view.
Media, keyboard and mouse events, and exposure summaries can be exported too, and Sensor Data can be converted to E D F files; section 04 shows where each one lives.
The rest is a pipeline in seven words: export, open, check, clean, merge, document, test.
The files spell the same participant and stimulus differently and count time from different moments, so every merge, the matching of rows from two files, needs a key made consistent first.
As you go you write a codebook (what each variable means), a cleaning log (every change, with its reason), and a Q A report (the counts and checks that show the data are what you think).

The worked example is a simulated study of 24 participants (P 01 to P 24) who watched two water bottle ads with eye tracking, facial expression analysis, skin conductance, and a survey; no person was recorded.
Time needed.
About 5 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (planning, exporting, opening files) in the first, 06 to 10 (checking, cleaning and merging, testing, writing) in the second
Equipment.
A lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1 for the export steps (section 04 and the last exercise); any computer with R 4.3 and RStudio, or Excel 365, for the rest
SoftwareiMotions Lab 11 point 1; R with read R, D plier, tidy R, purr, string R, G G plot 2, L M E 4, and L M E R test; Excel (365 or 2021 for X lookup)
Data files.
The simulated export bundle (simulated export bundle dot zip, 18 files in 8 folders), prepare data dot R, analysis dot R, their outputs, and the Excel workbook, in the site's data folder
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need this page and, for section 04 and the last exercise, a lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1; nothing else beyond knowing how to open a file.
If you did Workshop 2 (eye tracking), Workshop 3 (facial expression), or Workshop 4 (skin conductance), you will recognize the A O I, F E A, and G S R exports; nothing here depends on them.
Sections 07 and 08 offer two routes, two R scripts or an Excel workbook, and neither assumes programming experience.
Terms with a dotted underline open a definition when you tap them.
Help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com; for a first look, read Export: Sensor Data.

Practice exports only on the vendor demonstration studies in the Library, never on a lab study with participants, and never type a participant's name into a file name, a folder name, or a respondent field.
The one rule this workshop keeps repeating Never edit a raw export.

Keep every file exactly as iMotions wrote it, in a raw folder you treat as read only (the lab manual's Raw Data folder "contains unmodified data directly from devices"), work on a copy or in code, and write every change in the cleaning log.
A hand edit leaves no trace: nobody, including you next month, can tell what changed or repeat it.
Say what an analysis ready data set is, name the seven export families of the worked example and what each holds, state the pipeline from export to test, and explain why a raw export is never edited.
From question to data plan
A test needs a table, and iMotions gives you screens and files.

Take three questions a marketing team might ask about two video ads: is brand recall higher when viewers looked at the logo; do viewers who show more joy like the ad more; do the ads raise skin conductance above a resting level?
Each sounds simple, and none can be answered from one export.
Written as hypotheses, testable answers that name the variables to be measured, they read:
Brand recall is more likely when the Logo A O I was fixated.
A fixation is a pause in which the eyes hold still on one spot; "fixated" means at least one fixation inside the Logo during the ad.
Recall is a survey answer.
More Joy goes with more liking.
Joy is the percent of time during the ad that aff decks scored Joy at the threshold of 50 or higher; liking is a survey answer from 1 to 7.
G S R Peaks Per Minute are higher during each ad than during the Baseline, a gray screen with a fixation cross shown before the ads.
Each hypothesis needs a measure from a sensor, and H 1 and H 2 also need an answer from the survey.

The data plan therefore asks four questions of every measure: which export holds it, what one row of that export describes, which key joins that row to the others, and what must happen in iMotions before the file exists.
The second question names the unit of analysis, and iMotions exports come at three units.

Sensor Data has one row per sample, one reading of one device at one moment: "every row of data in the export file refers to a unique moment on the timeline," so a 60 hertz Aurora adds 60 rows a second and a Shimmer at 128 hertz adds 128.
The metrics files give one row "for each respondent and each stimulus" (and each scene or annotation): participant by stimulus.
The full survey response gives one row per respondent: the participant.
Two warnings go with this table.

First, the A O I identifier columns, the F E A metric columns, and the R export file names used in the bundle are not printed in the manuals; the worked example models them, and the Items to verify list (section 11) says so.
Second, the table names one key per file, but no two files spell it alike.

The respondent is Respondent Name in the R metrics and annotation files, Respondent in the survey, Respondent Name in the data quality file, and the file name plus the hash Respondent Name line in Sensor Data; the stimulus is Label, Source Stimuli Name, Stim Name, or Stimulus Name.
The clocks differ too: Sensor Data counts from the recording start, the R metrics from "the start of the study," and the annotation export from the stimulus onset.
Every join therefore starts by renaming the keys to one spelling and checking that every participant appears once in every file (sections 06 and 07).
The unit of analysis also decides the test.
The iMotions article General Data Analysis and Interpretation offers a decision chart (below) that starts from "Are your independent variables discrete or continuous?"
H 3 compares two conditions, an ad and the Baseline, measured on the same participants.
It follows the discrete branch to "Are your experimental conditions/samples independent?"
, answers No, and ends at "Repeated measures t-test", also called a paired t test, which asks whether the mean of each participant's difference (ad minus Baseline) differs from zero.
That test needs both values of each participant side by side, matched by the participant key; a file with one row per sample, or one average per stimulus, cannot give it.

H 2 lands on the continuous side (Pearson's r correlation or Simple Regression), but each participant contributes two pairs of values, one per ad, which the chart does not consider; H 1 has a yes or no variable on both sides, which it does not cover.
Section 08 explains the tests the plan uses, and Workshop 8 goes further.
The word aggregate means two things in iMotions, and only one of them belongs in a test.
The Introduction to Databasing article calls the summary measures per sensor "aggregate data" (figure below), such as peaks per minute for a stimulus.

Each summarizes the samples of one recording, so it is still one value per participant and stimulus, and the article recommends, "for the highest data fidelity," a "stimulus by participant" table in which "each column holds entries from a unique data source."
That is the table this workshop builds.
The other meaning is an average over people.

The A O I metrics table in iMotions shows values "averaged across all respondents in the current segment," where a segment is the group of respondents an analysis includes, and the aggregated A O I file, SurveyStatistics dot T X T, and the aggregate annotation file are aggregated exports of the same kind.
One number per stimulus or question cannot vary between participants, so there is nothing in it to test, and it was computed over everyone in the analysis before any exclusion rule.
As the Areas of Interest (A O I's) article puts it, "For statistical comparison, we recommend exporting the Individual A O I metrics."
Keep the aggregated files as checks: recomputed from the individual files, they must agree (section 06).
The table the tests need is tidy: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each kind of observational unit is its own table.
Here that means two tables.
The long table has one row per participant and stimulus (Baseline, Ad A, Ad B), with every measure for that pair in a column.

The wide table has one row per participant, with a column per measure and stimulus (Peaks Per Minute during Baseline, during Ad A, and during Ad B) and the answers that belong to the person, such as the attitude score.
Advice for spreadsheets points the same way: one header row, one thing in a cell, consistent codes, no calculations or color in the raw data, a data dictionary, and backups.
Here is the single most important idea of this workshop.
Every export answers one question at one unit of analysis, and an analysis needs several exports joined on keys that the exports spell differently and on clocks that start at different moments.

Data preparation is therefore a planned, logged, repeatable procedure, not a round of hand edits: plan which export holds which measure before collection, write the exclusion rules first, keep the raw exports untouched, read every file as text from a header found by rule, audit the keys against the session log, reshape, join, apply the rules, and write the codebook, the cleaning log, and the Q A report as you go.
Saving the raw data, recording every processing step, and giving every record a unique identifier are among the good enough practices in scientific computing (Wilson and colleagues
, 2017), and a collaborator should receive the raw data, the tidy data, a codebook, and the exact recipe from one to the other.
Guides to creating data dictionaries (Buchanan and colleagues
, 2021) and to documenting data automatically with the codebook package for R show how far a codebook can go; the one in this workshop is a plain C S V file.
One caution: the finished table links measures; it does not show what a viewer felt.
Joy at 50 or higher is a facial expression score, a peak is a change in skin conductance, and a fixation is where the eyes rested.
The General Data Analysis and Interpretation article warns against reading a mental process backward from a signal; section 10 returns to that warning.

Turn three questions into hypotheses; name for each measure the export that holds it, the unit of analysis, the key, and what must happen first; tell a summary within a recording from an average over people; and describe the tidy target and the documented procedure that produces it.
Planning the data before collection
Most data problems are made before the first participant sits down: a name typed two ways, a rerun nobody wrote down, a rule chosen after the results.

iMotions copies whatever was typed into every export, so the Data Handling article asks you to "name anything and everything that will show up in your exports" and to rename stimuli "before you begin data collection."
This section plans folders and file names, the rules, respondent names and the session log, the windows the exports are cut into, and storage.

The lab manual (section 8.2) prescribes one folder per project, /Research Data/Project Name/, with Raw Data/ (E E G, Eye Tracking, G S R, and Behavioral subfolders), Processed Data/, Analysis/, Documentation/ (Consent Forms, I R B Documents, Session Notes), and Backups/.
Raw Data "contains unmodified data directly from devices," and the split "separates raw vs processed clearly, preventing accidental overwriting."

Project doc 06 proposes a fuller study folder, from 00 Admin to 06 Deliverables, with the session log in 03 Collection and the exports by sensor in 04 Data Exports; it is a proposal, and whether the lab adopts it is on the Items to verify list.
The simulated bundle keeps one folder per export family, 01 Sensor Data to 08 Session Log.
The manual (section 8.1) also fixes data file names: ProjectID ParticipantID Date Device Version dot E X T, for example MFC2025 P001 20250930 E E G v1.edf.

The participant I D is "zero-padded" and the same "across all of a participant's files"; the date is year, month, and day; the device is E E G, G S R, Eye, or "Combined" for a merged data set; the version is v1 for raw files and v2 for processed ones; and names "avoid spaces or special characters."

The post-session checklist (section 7.1.7) shows the same example without the version (MFC2025 P001 20250930 E E G dot C S V); until the lab settles that conflict, follow 8.1 and keep the question on the Items to verify list.

Choose the width of the code before the first session: the manual pads to three digits (P001) and the simulated study to two (P 01 to P 24), and to a computer P 1, P 01, and P001 are three different keys.
Names matter inside iMotions too.

A Sensor Data file appears to be named with a running number and the respondent name (screenshots show files such as 001 A dot C S V; the pattern is inferred, so verify it), and the respondent name is repeated in the hash Respondent Name line and in a column of every metrics, survey, data quality, and annotation export.
A real name typed into iMotions travels into every file.
An exclusion rule is a written condition under which a participant or a value is left out.
The protocol of the simulated study, dated 2026 to 11 to 09 (simulated), fixed three before collection:
Use only recordings that the session log marks Use recording equals Yes.

Exclude a participant from all analyses when Eye tracking Quality is below 90 percent (lab manual Appendix D: "Eye tracking: >90 percent valid gaze samples") or Affectiva aff decks Quality is below 80 percent (the lab's face rule, used in Workshop 3) on Ad A or Ad B.
For G S R analyses only, a stimulus is missing when Signal Duration (milliseconds) is below 80 percent of Duration (milliseconds).
Signal Duration counts the signal "without gaps (if there are gaps longer than 4 seconds)."

Each rule names its column and its threshold, so a script can apply it and anyone can check the result, and the rules separate two kinds of loss: R 2 removes a participant from every test, R 3 removes one G S R value from the G S R test only.
Why write them before collection?
Because a rule chosen after seeing the data can be chosen, even without intent, to produce a result.
Undisclosed flexibility in data collection and analysis, including which observations to exclude, allows presenting almost anything as significant.
Writing the plan down before the data exist is preregistration, one of the measures in a manifesto for reproducible science (Munafò and colleagues
, 2017); and where several processing choices are defensible, a multiverse analysis reports the result under each of them, which increases transparency.
The iMotions article General Data Analysis and Interpretation gives the same advice: "have a clear research question, a hypothesis, and an analysis plan before data collection."
In iMotions a respondent is one entry in a study's respondent list, with one recording; the participant is the person.
Usually the two match one to one, but not always.
Name every respondent with the participant code, never with a name.

The lab manual (section 2.4) says "Never label data files or reports with a participant's name," asks for an I D like "P001" rather than "Jane Doe," and keeps the key that links codes to names separately; the iMotions privacy F A Q says "Use anonymous I Ds as respondent names."
This is de-identification.

Fix the one spelling of the code (capital P, the chosen number of digits, no spaces) before the first session, because names are typed by hand and every export copies the name as it stood at the moment of export.
The respondent details, Name, Gender, Age, and Group, are set when a respondent is created and can be changed later (click the study, then the respondent name, then Respondent Details, then Update).

They go into the hash info lines of Sensor Data and into the R metrics, survey, and annotation exports, so fill them in at the session: a field left as it was is exported with its default value as if it were data (the Data Collection Overview screenshot shows Gender Other, Age 0, and Group Default before anything is typed).
The simulated study puts the order of the ads in Group: odd participants saw Ad A first (AB) and even participants Ad B first (BA), a counterbalanced order, so the order travels into every export.
A change typed after an export does not reach a file already exported; export again.
Sometimes a recording must be repeated, for example when the eye tracker calibration fails in the live view.
A rerun is a new respondent for the same participant.

The simulated study names it with the code and a suffix, such as P04 rerun, so that two recordings never share a name; whether iMotions even accepts two respondents with one name in one study is an item to verify.
The only place that says which recording counts is the session log, the operators' table of every recording.

The simulated log has one row per recording, 25 rows for 24 participants (simulated), with the columns Participant I D, iMotions respondent name, Recording, Session date, Start time, Seat, Computer, Operator, Order (typed in Group), Shimmer unit, Aurora calibration, Use recording, and Notes.

It is modeled on the log Project doc 06 proposes, with one row per recording instead of one per participant so that a rerun has a row of its own, and it serves the lab manual's post-session step, "Update any data log Excel with the new entry."
The session log is the roster of the study, the list of participants who should appear in every file, and the table that maps each respondent name to a participant code (section 07).

The R metrics files give results "for every respondent included in the analysis and for every stimulus, scene, or annotation present in the study (not only for the entire stimulus duration as in the Replay)."
Two consequences follow.
A time window you want measured must exist in the study as a stimulus, a scene, or an annotation before the notebooks run and the files are exported.
And the respondents in an export are the respondents in the analysis.
A Stimulus annotation applies to every respondent who saw the stimulus ("only available for stimuli that can be aggregated"); a Respondent annotation applies to one respondent.
In the R metrics files annotations "serve as 'measurement windows'."

The simulated study plans one: a Stimulus annotation named End Card on each ad, from 25,000 to 30,000 milliseconds after the ad starts (simulated), so that the last five seconds of each ad get rows of their own.

An annotation can have several instances, and a scene, a named interval of a dynamic stimulus such as a screen recording or a website, can have several fragments; the G S R export writes one row "for each respondent and each stimulus divided by scene divided by scene fragment divided by annotation divided by annotation instance," so decide before export which rows you want.
The analysis decides who is in the export.

A new analysis starts with Add Analysis beside the study in the Library and four steps: Segmentation Settings, Segmentation Criteria (Gender, Age, Flow, Group, and advanced options such as data quality metrics), Signal Processing, and Select Stimuli ("all stimuli, by default").

Survey exports "only consider the respondents and slides included in the analysis," and the Export: Survey data article advises to "first create a 'master-analysis' (including all respondents/all slides)."

The plan follows that advice for every analysis export: one master analysis with every respondent and every stimulus, and the rules applied afterward in code, where each exclusion is logged and can be undone.
Leaving a respondent out of the iMotions analysis instead removes the person from every file with no line in the cleaning log to say why.
Segments still help after the rules, for example to show a client an aggregate of the analysis sample only.

A legacy option filters an analysis's respondents with a file: choose "C S V filter" in the respondent panel, browse to a file that holds "the desired respondent names in a column," say whether it has a "Header on first line," and give the "Column containing respondent name."
The article is marked Legacy, so whether the filter still exists in Lab 11 point 1 is an item to verify.
The lesson the lab learned the hard way The lab once lost the studies on a computer that became unavailable and recovered those that had been saved as study zip files.
A study that exists only inside one computer's iMotions database is one hardware failure away from loss; so are exports that were never saved anywhere else.
A study zip is the whole study saved as one dot zip file: right-click the study, then Save To File (".

zip file (for backing up studies/data or transferring studies to other computers)"), or save every study at once with Tools, then Save all studies to file, then Backup; File, then Load Study From File, brings it back.

Save it to a local drive and copy it afterward, because the iMotions article warns that saving study files straight to external drives or cloud folders can corrupt them, and avoid "extracting, unzipping, or making edits."

The lab manual turns this into a routine (section 8.3): back up "Immediately after each session" to the lab server, at the end of the day to an encrypted external drive or the approved cloud (One Drive for Business), weekly in full offline, and monthly off site; "Document these backups"; and keep "at least 3 copies of any irreplaceable raw data."
In practice: after each collection day, save the study zip and the exports into the study folder, mark the raw exports read only, and copy both.
"Always de-identify data before cloud if possible."

Face video needs extra care: the Data Handling article suggests exporting "a version of your study without facial recordings," and Save To File can exclude the camera recordings, but only after any post processing of the videos is finished, as the iMotions privacy F A Q notes.
Keep raw data "at least 7 years" and processed data 5 years (section 8.4), and "Always check the I R B protocol" in case it sets another period.
Before you promise a participant anything about storage or sharing, read on the privacy implications of eye tracking and the practical tips for ethical data sharing.

Set up folders and file names under the lab rule, write exclusion rules before collection and say why, name respondents with codes and record every recording and rerun in a session log, plan the annotations, scenes, and master analysis that decide the rows of every export, and plan the backups that keep raw data safe.
The worked example
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page, the first deliverable of any study in this lab.
Below is the simulated Multimodal Ad Study as a one page plan, a screen based lab study like those of Workshops 2 to 4; read it as a template for your own.
After it comes the export bundle the study produced: the files you will open, check, clean, and merge in the rest of the workshop.
Everything about this study is simulated No person was recorded, no camera or sensor was switched on, and no file from a lab study was used.
One script, make simulated data dot P Y (seed 20271231), wrote every file; the participants are codes, P 01 to P 24; and no number in this workshop may be quoted as a finding.
Every file starts with one line, "# simulated Data", that a real export does not have, and all row numbers in the workshop materials count that line.

Among 24 participants (simulated) who watch two 30 seconds video ads for reusable water bottles in the lab, is brand recall higher when the Logo was fixated, do participants whose faces show more Joy like the ad more, and do the ads raise skin conductance peaks above a resting Baseline?
H 1: brand recall is more likely when the Logo was fixated (A O I by survey).
H 2: more Joy goes with more liking (F E A by survey).
H 3: G S R Peaks Per Minute are higher during each ad than during Baseline (G S R).
Every test is two tailed at alpha point 0 5.
One participant at a time at the lab desktop (Key 0002), November 16 to 20, 2026 (simulated dates).
Within subjects: everyone sees both ads.
The order is counterbalanced, odd participants AB and even participants BA, and typed by the operator into Group.

Smart Eye Aurora (60 hertz); the respondent camera with Affectiva aff decks (about 30 frames per second); a Shimmer 3 G S R plus (G S R and P P G, 128 hertz), one of the lab's two units, Shimmer 3 to 8956 or a second unit called Shimmer 3 B here (a placeholder name).

Instructions (self paced); Baseline (a 60 seconds gray screen with a fixation cross); Ad A (30 seconds, the fictional brand Altavo, a hiking scene); Ad B (30 seconds, the fictional brand Brenlow, a cycling scene); Questionnaire (an iMotions survey slide).
All lengths are those of the simulated study.
On each ad, active for the whole ad: Logo (top left, small), Product (center), and Headline (bottom).
One Stimulus annotation per ad, End Card, from 25,000 to 30,000 milliseconds after the ad starts (simulated).

Question I Ds Liking A and Liking B (1 to 7); Recall A and Recall B (which brand was advertised in the hiking ad and in the cycling ad: Altavo, Brenlow, Caskel, Dorvane, or I do not remember), scored 1 for the advertised brand and 0 for any other answer by an answer key written in the protocol; A T T 1, A T T 2, and A T T 3 R (attitude toward reusable water bottles, 1 to 7), where A T T 3 R is a reverse worded item, recoded as 8 minus the answer before the three are averaged; and PI (purchase intention, 1 to 7).
Name: the participant code, with rerun added for a rerun.
Gender and Age as the participant gives them.
Group: AB or BA.
Written in the protocol on 2026 to 11 to 09 (simulated), before collection.
R 1: use only recordings the session log marks for use.
R 2: exclude a participant from all analyses when eye tracking quality is below 90 percent or aff decks quality below 80 percent on either ad.
R 3: for G S R analyses only, a stimulus is missing when Signal Duration is below 80 percent of Duration.

Analysis exports from one master analysis with every respondent and stimulus: Sensor Data (Baseline, Ad A, and Ad B; eye tracking, aff decks, and G S R) for the raw data checks; the A O I Metrics Export, individual and aggregated files, for H 1; the F E A Metrics Export (threshold 50; Joy, Engagement, and Brow Furrow) for H 2; G S R Peak Metrics for H 3 and R 3; the Full Survey response and Survey Statistics for the survey items; the annotation export for the End Card window and the clock checks.
From the study: the data quality file for R 2.
From the operators: the session log for R 1.
H 1: Fisher's exact test on the 2 by 2 table of Logo fixated by brand recalled, pooled over the two ads, repeated for each ad, and checked with a mixed model.
H 2: a mixed model of liking on Joy (per 10 percentage points) and the ad, with correlations for each ad.
H 3: paired t tests of each ad against Baseline with the effect size d z, Wilcoxon signed rank tests as checks, and Holm's correction over the two ads.
prepare data.

R (21 Step blocks, step 0 to step 20) writes analysis ready long dot C S V (one row per participant and stimulus; 72 rows and 29 columns, simulated; include equals 1 marks the analysis sample), analysis ready wide dot C S V (one row per participant; 24 rows and 34 columns), codebook dot C S V (57 rows), cleaning log dot C S V (20 entries), and qa report dot T X T.

analysis dot R writes analysis output dot T X T, simulated test results dot C S V, and simulated descriptives dot C S V. The Excel route builds the core of the same table in simulated data prep dot X L S X, guided by excel walkthrough dot M D.

The two analysis ready tables with the codebook, the cleaning log, and the Q A report as supplementary materials; a data preparation paragraph with counts at every step and a participant flow table; the three tests in A P A style; and a plain language summary for the client (sections 09 and 10).
The test names return in section 08.

In brief: Fisher's exact test asks whether two yes or no variables are related and stays exact in small samples; a mixed model gives each participant a starting level of his or her own, so that two observations from one person are not counted as two people; the Wilcoxon signed rank test repeats the paired comparison on ranks; d z is the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the differences; and Holm's correction adjusts the p values when two tests answer one hypothesis.
The iMotions screens show measures like these, and they are for looking, not for testing.
The two screenshots below come from vendor example studies, not from the simulated study.

The A O I metrics table shows each metric averaged over the respondents of the analysis (Respondent base 8 in the vendor example), one number per A O I; the Replay window shows one respondent's G S R peak metrics for a whole stimulus (Peaks per minute equals 3.87 in the vendor example).

The plan needs neither: H 1 takes one Logo value per participant and ad from the individual A O I file, and H 3 one Peaks Per Minute value per participant and stimulus from the G S R export, which also covers scenes and annotations.
The bundle, simulated export bundle dot zip, holds 18 files in 8 folders, as the lab would receive them after collection.

Its read me dot M D states for every file what is documented, meaning that an iMotions article or screenshot prints the name or layout, and what is modeled, meaning that the workshop chose it where the manuals are silent and it must be verified on the lab computer.
The table condenses read me section 3; all row counts are simulated.
Read the row counts as a first check, not as trivia.

Some are plain multiples of the design (144 equals 24 participants by 2 ads by 3 A O I's, simulated), and some are not (170 rows of G S R metrics, 122 rows of data quality, 510 rows of F E A metrics); section 06 asks you to explain every count before you trust a file.
The Sensor Data folder holds six participants only, to keep the bundle small, and six are enough for the raw data checks.
What does modeled mean for you?
A modeled name is a careful guess from the manuals, and code that expects it will fail, or worse, read the wrong column, if the real export differs.

Before real data go through this pipeline, export a demo study on the lab computer, compare each file's names, separators, and header lines with the bundle, and correct the script and the codebook where they differ.
read me section 5 lists ten items to verify, from the Sensor Data separator to the meaning of Start (milliseconds) and the Excel settings on the lab computers; section 11 repeats them.

Write the one page plan of a multimodal lab study, match each hypothesis and rule to the files that answer it, read the bundle's file list with its row counts, and say which names and layouts are documented and which are modeled and must be verified.
Getting every export out
iMotions does not hand over one data file.

It writes many exports, and each answers one question at one unit of analysis: Sensor Data holds one row per sample, a metrics export one row per respondent and interval, the survey matrix one row per respondent.
The three hypotheses of section 03 need five export families plus the lab's session log, so this section takes every family in turn.
The word "Export" appears in several places, so start with the map.
The first three rows were confirmed on the lab computer on October 10, 2026 (iMotions Lab 11 point 1, build 4 7 1 3 6).
The other paths come from articles written for releases 8.0 to 10.0.7, and every 11 point 1 label not yet confirmed is on the Items to verify list (section 11).

Three rules for every export (1) Export from one master analysis that includes every respondent and every stimulus; the exclusion rules are applied later, in code (section 07), never by leaving people out of an analysis.
(2) Never type a participant's name where iMotions can see it: codes only, with the key that links codes to names stored apart from the data (lab manual 2.4).

(3) Copy every export, unchanged, into the study's raw data folder on the day it is made, and back it up (lab manual 8.2 and 8.3): the lab once lost the studies on a computer that became unavailable and recovered only those saved as study zip files.

Cleaning and merging

Opened correctly, the exports are still separate tables that cannot be analyzed together: their keys are named and sometimes spelled differently, some rows belong to recordings that must not be used, and some answers need scoring before they mean anything.
This section turns them into two analysis ready tables with prepare data dot R. Every change is a line of code and a line in the cleaning log; nothing is typed into a file by hand.
That is the advice of the data management literature: keep raw data untouched, script every step, and describe every variable.
Hand edits are where errors hide, and researchers report many data management mistakes of their own.
Steps 14 to 16, which check the clocks, the raw samples, and data quality, are explained in section 06; this section walks through the steps that change the data.

The recall items store the chosen label (1 to 5), not correct or wrong, which is why iMotions reports a meaningless Recall A "Average" of 2.42; they are scored against the answer key written before collection (Label1, Altavo, for Ad A; Label2, Brenlow, for Ad B).

Cronbach's alpha describes how consistently the items of one scale move together: alpha equals k divided by (k - 1) x (1 - sum of the item variances divided by variance of the sum).
